reason: Artemis III must land near the south pole, where the ice and the long sunlight are.
source: "Land within 6 deg latitude of the South Pole". NASA, Artemis Human Landing System Update (2024), NTRS 20240009596, https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20240009596

reason: A lander on a steep slope can tip over; NASA sets the limit at 10 degrees for the landing area.
source: "Surface slope for landing (100m): <10 deg". NASA, Artemis Human Landing System Update (2024), NTRS 20240009596, https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20240009596. We measure across 120 m, the finest the map allows, and take the steepest side.

unit: % of the ground with slope under 20 deg
reason: Astronauts in suits cannot walk on ground steeper than 20 degrees, and walk at most about 2 km.
source: "Surface slope limit for EVA (2km): <20 deg" and "No EVAs can occur in black areas". NASA, Artemis Human Landing System Update (2024), NTRS 20240009596, https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20240009596. The 50 % share is a team choice: NASA gives the slope and the distance, not how much of the ground must be walkable.

unit: % of time, NASA PGDA long-run average
reason: The crew needs daylight for the whole 6.5-day stay, for power, warmth and to see.
source: "Artemis III will require the surface to be lit for the duration of the surface stay". NASA, Artemis Human Landing System Update (2024), NTRS 20240009596, https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20240009596. Stay of 6.5 days: NASA release of 19 Aug 2022. The 25 % screen is a team choice: of 192 points we modelled above it, 99.0 % have a 6.5-day stretch with Sun and Earth both up. Each zone is then checked with our own model.

unit: % of time, NASA PGDA long-run average
reason: With no relay satellite, the radio only works while Earth is above the skyline.
source: "Direct with Earth (DWE) communication; assume no comm relay is available"; the NASA map removes "Earth visibility < 25%". NASA, Artemis Human Landing System Update (2024), NTRS 20240009596, https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20240009596

ideal: a 100 m x 100 m box that passes
reason: The lander can only be steered to within about 100 m, so the whole box around the target must be safe.
source: "Human Landing Accuracy Requirements 100 m x 100 m". NASA, Artemis Human Landing System Update (2024), NTRS 20240009596, https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20240009596. One cell of our 120 m map covers the box.

reason: More sunlight means more solar power and fewer cold nights.
source: Team choice of the 70 % ideal: only the best ridges reach it. Data: NASA GSFC PGDA product 69, https://pgda.gsfc.nasa.gov/products/69 (Mazarico et al. 2011).

reason: More time with Earth in view means more time to talk to mission control.
source: Team choice of the 70 % ideal. NASA: "regions with greater Earth visibility are preferred" (NTRS 20250011660, https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20250011660). Data: PGDA product 69.

reason: Flatter ground leaves a margin for boulders and small craters the map cannot see.
source: Apollo lunar module design surface: "a mean surface slope of 6 deg or less" (NASA TN D-6850, https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/19720018253). 5 deg is a team choice just inside it.

reason: Water ice may survive only where the Sun never shines, so the science is in the permanent shadows nearby.
source: Walking radius: "PSRs located within 2 km, the current radial limit for astronauts without a rover" (Wueller et al. 2026, doi:10.1029/2025JE009434). Rover reach: "up to 20 km without recharging" (NASA, NTRS 20230002802). Shadow = PGDA average sunlight of 0, patches of 1 km2 or more (team choice).

unit: % of the ground with slope under 20 deg
reason: The more of the surroundings the crew can walk, the more they can explore.
source: Team choice of the 95 % ideal; the 20 deg and 2 km come from NASA, Artemis Human Landing System Update (2024), NTRS 20240009596, https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20240009596.

unit: K, yearly average 2 cm below the surface
reason: Very cold ground means the spot is nearly always dark, and hardware needs more heating.
source: 110 K: "surfaces below 110 K capable of cold trapping water" (Williams et al. 2019, doi:10.1029/2019JE006028). 150 K ideal is a team choice. Data: LRO Diviner Polar Resource Product, https://pds-geosciences.wustl.edu/lro/urn-nasa-pds-lro_diviner_derived1/data_derived_prp/ (a thermal model on a ~0.5 km mesh).

reason: Most landers are built for one lunar day and die in a long night; a short night can be survived on batteries.
source: Ideal: NASA's rover goal to "survive an extended lunar night duration of at least 85 hours" (NTRS 20230002802). Reject: "Non-polar latitudes night durations ~354 hours" (NASA Glenn, NTRS 20210026571). Computed by our own model at each zone's best cell.

reason: While Earth is below the skyline the lander is out of contact.
source: Team choice, anchored on NASA's description: "Earth is in a 2-week cycle: visible two weeks, not visible two weeks" (NASA, Artemis Human Landing System Update (2024), NTRS 20240009596, https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20240009596). Computed by our own model at each zone's best cell.

reason: Radio takes about 1.2 to 1.36 seconds to cross from the Moon to Earth from every site, so it cannot rank sites; a delay under about 1.16 seconds is physically impossible.
source: Light time from our ephemeris (JPL DE421). Distance range 357,000 to 407,000 km: NASA NSSDC Moon Fact Sheet, https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/moonfact.html

reason: High ground sees over its neighbours, which is why the best-lit spots are peaks and crater rims.
source: LOLA LDEM_75S_120M, PDS Geosciences Node. Not scored by itself: its effect is already in the sunlight and Earth numbers.
